newsitem.title: UK: Police try to break up green protest at Conoco office.
newsitem.headline: Police try to break up green protest at Conoco office.

text.p: Police have arrived at the London offices of U.S. oil company Conoco and are attempting to remove Greenpeace activists occupying the building, a Greenpeace spokeswoman said.
The environmental group is protesting against Conoco's plans to explore for oil in the Atlantic Ocean.
Greenpeace said that 15 activists gained access to the central London office and chained themselves to various parts of the building at around 8.00 a.m. (0700 GMT) on Wednesday morning.
"The police have turned up and cordoned the whole area off and have removed a small number of activists in the building that weren't locked on," the Greenpeace spokeswoman said.
She said that the remaining activists were firmly chained to parts of the building and would be more difficult to budge.
Another 12 protesters, some standing inside oil barrels, were blockading the front of the building. Above them they have erected a banner saying: "Stop climate change - No new oil".
Conoco is a unit of U.S. chemicals giant Du Pont Co. It retails petrol in Britain under the brand name Jet.
The company won the right to explore for oil in the Atlantic Ocean to the west of the Shetland Islands in Britain's seventeenth offshore licensing round.
"The activists inside the building are refusing to leave until Jet gives Greenpeace an assurance that it will not explore for new oil in the Atlantic Frontier," Greenpeace said in a statement.
A spokeswoman for Conoco said they were speaking to protesters and listening to their concerns. She said a statement would be made later this morning.
Greenpeace has made the Atlantic frontier the focus of its climate change campaign in Britain.
Oil companies discovered commercial quantities in deep Atlantic waters five years ago, and first flows from British Petroleum's Foinaven field are expected late this summer.
But Greenpeace says that fossil fuels must remain in the ground if carbon dioxide emissions that cause global warming are to be curbed.
"Searching for oil...against a backdrop of climate change is madness. The solution is simple, Jet must say no to new oil to help save the climate," Greenpeace said in a statement.
In April, Greenpeace protesters raided BP's Aberdeen office in an attempt to install solar panels on the roof.
It scored a major victory in 1995 when it forced Anglo-Dutch oil giant Shell to rethink its plans to ditch the Brent Spar oil platform at sea.
A high profile campaign involved Greenpeace attempts to block the platform being towed to its Atlantic dumping site and a boycott of Shell petrol stations in Europe.
